results.final_answer: Based on internal policy documentation: [appeals_policy.md] Appeals for timely-filing denials (CO-29) are rarely successful and should only be filed when the provider has documented proof of on-time submission, such as a clearinghouse transmission report with a timestamp before the filing deadline.; [claims_submission_policy.md] Medicare requires claims to be filed within 365 days of the date of service. Commercial payers - including Aetna, BlueCross BlueShield, and UnitedHealthcare - require timely filing within 90 days of the date of service. A claim submitted after the applicable window is denied with code CO-29 and is not eligible for a timely-filing exception except in cases of documented payer system outages.; [claims_submission_policy.md] Corrected claims (resubmissions fixing an administrative error) must reference the original claim number and be submitted within 60 days of the original denial notice, or they are treated as new claims subject to the standard timely filing window.

Based on internal policy documentation: [appeals_policy.md] A first-level appeal must be filed within 180 days of the denial notice date. If the first-level appeal is upheld, a second-level appeal must be filed within 60 days of the first-level decision. If the second-level appeal is also upheld, the claim may proceed to an independent external review within 120 days, where available under the payer's plan type.

Based on internal policy documentation: [hipaa_privacy_policy.md] A suspected breach of unsecured PHI affecting 500 or more individuals must be reported to the Department of Health and Human Services and to affected individuals within 60 days of discovery, per the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule. Breaches affecting fewer than 500 individuals may be reported in an annual log but must still notify affected individuals within 60 days.

Based on internal policy documentation: [hipaa_privacy_policy.md] Access to protected health information follows the HIPAA minimum necessary standard: staff should be given access to only the PHI needed to perform their specific role, and no more. Viewers may see redacted, aggregated claims metrics only. Operators may look up individual claims and denial details for casework, and every such lookup is written to the audit log. Admins may additionally generate cross-payer remediation plans that reference aggregate denial patterns.

Based on internal policy documentation: [prior_authorization_policy.md] If a service is rendered without the required authorization, the payer may grant a retroactive authorization only if the request is submitted within 30 days of the date of service and includes clinical documentation showing the service was medically necessary at the time it was rendered. A retroactive authorization, once granted, is the basis for a CO-197 appeal.; [denial_management_policy.md] Code CO-197 means precertification or authorization was absent at the time of service. This is an authorization denial. If authorization can be obtained retroactively from the payer, the claim should be appealed with the retroactive authorization number attached.; [claims_submission_policy.md] Medicare requires claims to be filed within 365 days of the date of service. Commercial payers - including Aetna, BlueCross BlueShield, and UnitedHealthcare - require timely filing within 90 days of the date of service. A claim submitted after the applicable window is denied with code CO-29 and is not eligible for a timely-filing exception except in cases of documented payer system outages.

Based on internal policy documentation: [denial_management_policy.md] Code CO-50 means the service is non-covered because it was not deemed a medical necessity. This is a clinical denial and requires a letter of medical necessity with supporting documentation from the treating provider before it can be appealed successfully.; [prior_authorization_policy.md] Medicare does not require prior authorization for knee arthroscopy in most cases, but does require supporting documentation of a medical necessity - typically imaging results and a trial of conservative treatment - to avoid a CO-50 denial.; [denial_management_policy.md] Code CO-16 means the claim or service lacks information needed for adjudication - this is an administrative denial and is almost always resolved by resubmitting with the missing field, most commonly a diagnosis code or a referring provider NPI.
